@graph.headline: Why Backtested Strategies Fail in Live Trading: 5 Gaps

acceptedAnswer.text: Because your backtest was a laboratory and live is the field. The backtest filled orders at the signal price with costs roughly estimated, on clean historical data, in one past market regime, while following the rules perfectly. Live differs in five ways: the execution gap (you fill at the market's price, not the signal price), the cost gap (real costs are larger and hide in spreads, charges, and taxes the backtest ignored), the data gap (live data is messy and your live signal path may differ), the regime gap (the market changed), and the trader gap (you do not follow the rules like the backtest did). Work through the five tests above; the failure is usually in one of them.

mainEntity.name: Why did my backtest show great results but I am losing money live?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on the tightness ratio: your average win divided by per-trade friction. For a swing trader with wide targets, a fraction of a percent of slippage is noise. For a scalper, half a point of slippage per trade can be the entire edge — and frequency multiplies it. For Indian option buyers there is an extra layer: backtests built on mid-prices, but live you buy the ask and sell the bid, paying the full spread every round trip — often larger than the average win on tight setups. Model slippage and spread explicitly; never trust the tool's default.

mainEntity.name: Does slippage really matter in backtesting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Entry slippage roughly balances out over many trades — you miss both ways. Stop-loss slippage is directional: gaps blow through stops in the losing direction. A backtest assuming exact stop fills systematically understates the worst losses. The fix is the stop-fill penalty: model stop exits with an extra adverse penalty and reconcile your actual stop fills against it on every trade.

mainEntity.name: Why do my stops get filled worse than my entries?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with realistic practitioner estimates for your instrument — liquid NIFTY options behave very differently from illiquid stock-option strikes — then run the double-cost stress test: double every cost, including slippage and the spread. If the strategy survives, it is robust to cost uncertainty. If it only works with perfect fills, it does not work. The exact numbers are estimates; the stress test matters more than any single figure.

mainEntity.name: How much slippage should I add to a backtest?

acceptedAnswer.text: In-sample, a strategy can memorize the sample's noise — patterns that existed by chance in that specific period. Out-of-sample is the first taste of data the strategy has never seen, and chance patterns do not repeat. The industry's published research points the same way: one widely discussed analysis of crowd-sourced strategies found backtest performance offered little predictive value for out-of-sample results, and in the McLean–Pontiff academic study, published predictors lost about 26% out-of-sample. (How strategies memorize noise — and how to detect it — gets its own chapter next week.)

mainEntity.name: Why do backtests work in-sample but fail out-of-sample?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some gap is normal — and most traders were never told that. One practitioner's calibration framework: live performance at 70–80% of the backtest is good, 50–70% is acceptable, below 50% is concerning, and a live strategy going negative when the backtest was positive needs action. If your gap is larger than the bands allow, work the five gaps above.

mainEntity.name: Why is there such a big gap between backtest and live performance?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The backtest never hesitated, never skipped a setup, never moved a stop, never revenge-traded. You will — and the moment you do, you are no longer trading the strategy the backtest validated. Forward-test at tiny size or on paper and measure your deviations from the plan before you size up. The strategy must survive the market and the person trading it.

mainEntity.name: Does a backtest account for emotions?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A backtest replays history — fast, but it carries all four structural gaps (execution, cost, data, regime). Paper trading runs forward, live, without capital — slow, but it removes look-ahead risk by construction and gives you real-time fills and real data messiness. The backtest asks "did this work in the past"; paper trading asks "does it work now, with me operating it." The honest funnel uses both: backtest, stress test, out-of-sample, paper, then live small.
